utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is there anything to be discussed before we resume the cross-examination of Mr. Carswell?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you wish it, I could briefly indicate our considered position in relation to the exhibits, the documentary exhibits in respect of -- perhaps I should not mention his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know what exhibits we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, having checked the transcript, it is necessary for the Prosecution to tender the documents and, therefore, we have followed the procedure which you suggested yesterday and excised the relevant passages. Perhaps my friends should have an opportunity to consider the appropriateness of those decisions before we formally tender them to you. In the meantime, as you may have noticed yesterday, Mr. President, I'm doing my best to have read on to the transcript either by myself or the witness the relevant passages from documents so as to avoid this issue arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. I then expect that you will hand out a copy of the document as you want to tender it to Ms. Pilipovic and Ms. Pilipovic will then have an opportunity to prepare what the position of the Defence will be and then they will finally take a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And Mr. President, by way of timetable, assuming that the present witness will be finished in the next 15 minutes or so, the next witness will be taken by Mr. Mundis and then I will take the witness following him, I anticipate, therefore, I will be back in the Trial Chamber well before 7.00 tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I would like to apologise for my involuntary absence yesterday, but since Mr. Ierace was standing and before he leaves, could he give us some answers to the question that we have been asking for some time. And the question is: To get an answer as to the documents that we defined, the documents that have been manipulated, interfered with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could an answer be given -- I think it was Mr. Stamp that dealt with the documents and you indicated yesterday that you would confer with Mr. Stamp or wait until he would be back in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Having clarified that issue yesterday, I made some enquiries and perhaps at the same time that we deal with the tender of the documents in relation to last witness, I could formally respond. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, if we will do that then later today. Then, Ms. Pilipovic, you are ready to resume the cross-examination of Mr. Carswell. Mr. Usher, could you please guide the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Carswell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it is not necessary, but may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief yesterday asked by my learned colleague you spoke about the meeting that you had with General Stanislav Galic. Could you please tell us when was it that you personally spoke with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. The instance when I was there, I was again as a number two, the sector commander, Commandant O'Keefe was leading the team and that would have been late March.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you say "late March" who was together with General Galic as other members of his team?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is not entirely clear on that, ma'am. On the -- I believe -- I believe there were one or -- I can't be sure. I have a recollection, I believe, of one major being there. I am afraid it is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Following that meeting or because of this meeting, did you compile a report following that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report dealing specifically with the meeting, ma'am, would have been compiled by the sector commander, Major O'Keefe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you personally never spoke to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at the time, and I wish I could give you the exact date, although I have it in my diary. I believe at the time I spoke with him and we were dealing with -- my points were more on the fire, the artillery fire or mortar fire that was falling close --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. Could you tell us when was that and where did this discussion take place when you spoke to General Galic. You say that you made a note of it in your diary.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did. Unfortunately, I don't have my diary in front of me. I believe it was -- I think it was 24 March.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us at that time when you spoke to General Galic who was with him then and where did this meeting, this conversation, this discussion take place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, ma'am I believe -- there was one staff officer, I think he was at the rank of major. It took place in Lukavica in a conference room which adjoined the UNMO quarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at the time when you spoke to him, when you said you had a conversation or discussion regarding the shelling, could you tell us specifically about which incident was it -- was the discussion about on that 24th of March when you met General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I spoke specifically about the shelling that was occurring around our OPs on the Papa side. The actually --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us of which operation -- observation points?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been any one of the three, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In which language did you speak to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Galic have an interpreter with him?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he did, but I cannot be sure. The interpreters were generally present.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Following this discussion, this meeting, did you compile a report?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I mentioned before, it would have been mentioned in my sitrep, but the sector commander would have made the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the time on the 24th of March when you spoke to General Galic did -- was your superior Mr. Cutler?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. It was in the Irish Army, Commandant O'Keefe, and as I mentioned before, without consulting my diary I am not exactly sure it was the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you are not certain that it was on the 24th, what do you mean by that? You are not sure that this took place on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without consulting my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At this meeting did your Commandant O'Keefe also attend?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, on both these meetings, there was your commander was with you, so you were never personally on your own with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite correct, however, I did have points that I would bring up on behalf of the military observers. The first meeting, was with the chief military observer. He accompanied me, I accompanied him; and the second meeting was with Commandant O'Keefe and I might add --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, at this first meeting, who was present for the team that you were a member of, who was the commander there, the commandant?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the team would have been me. I was with the chief military observer and my commandant was not present at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at the time also have the rank of a major?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you as a major, was it possible for you to speak to the general as a Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I might add on a number of occasions, we attempted to put together meetings with either General Galic or his staff, his senior staff, and were unable to do so. And I understand -- I understand not being able to do so in that there was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at the time when you spoke either at one or the other meeting, did you hand a written protest to General Galic? Did you inform him in written form about what the subject of your protest was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that protest note was handed by the -- on one occasion, by Commandant O'Keefe, and I am not sure what the chief military observer, if a protest was handled -- sorry, handed over or not. I do know that Lieutenant Cutler, although I don't have them with me at all, I know that Major Cutler sent some letters of protest. Colonel Cutler.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Galic answered these letters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I do not. But I will answer that when we delivered our verbal comments to his staff and on the occasion that I had the opportunity to speak with him that what I had asked for was actioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether General Galic answered in writing your protest, do you know anything about it; if you can answer by yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your diary, on the 24th of January, and we spoke about it yesterday and I asked you a question about the oxygen bottles that were used to transport gunpowder, escorted by UNPROFOR, and you made a note of that in your diary of the 24th of January. Could you tell us, did you undertake any measures to find out who agreed on behalf of the UNPROFOR to have the gunpowder transported into Sarajevo in oxygen bottles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend has informed the witness of an entry in his diary. I think it would be appropriate, it would be appropriate for my friend, my learned colleague to show that entry to the witness so he can check its correctness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday -- I showed this yesterday. Mr. Carswell had the document before him. This is the document we spoke about yesterday and because of the time, I just want this to be more efficient and I believe that Mr. Carswell confirmed that he knew about this incident. It is page number 9 and the document is 752, entry for the 24th of January. And I just wanted to be a little more precise and also to ask the witness to be a little more precise and to answer whether he personally, as a member of the UN team, take any steps to find out who gave authorisation for this, approval for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, in the translation, it said "diary." I now do understand that you are referring to the monthly report of -- of the month of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, do you remember yesterday we spoke about this date, the 24th of January, when in that monthly sitrep it was established that the Lima side UNMOs were called to the Blazuj hospital to witness that two of the oxygen bottles delivered by the UNPROFOR were found to contain gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text reads that it is UNHCR and not UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am looking at the original text as well, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you quoted it almost, apart from the saying "UNPROFOR" instead of UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the translation it says UNPROFOR. I apologise. I am reading the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, did you, following this incident, receive and did you ask for certain information and certain checks?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not and I will answer why. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge -- yes, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We demanded of the UNMOs as observers, and as I mentioned yesterday, the action taken in that case, we immediately passed our observations on to the CivPol, I believe it was the CivPol. And it was handled by them. We had no means to do an inspection, nor any mandate to do any inspection, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that the transport of gunpowder in oxygen bottle was known as "Operation Oxygen", did you have that information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge which members of your team, of the UNMO team -- who discovered that there was gunpowder in oxygen bottles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNMO team did not discover. They were called on to the scene once it was discovered. However, I was not there, nor do I remember the time lapse between the delivery of the bottles and the discovery.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you later, during your stay, during your mandate, find out that such transport of oxygen bottles had been done earlier as well, escorted by UNPROFOR, and that it was used by the BH army and that it was used for the manufacturing of weapons, did you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not. And I would be very surprised if they -- would have been very surprised, if they would -- if information like that would be passed along.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why would you be surprised by that? Could you give us that answer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a war going on. I don't believe we would have or should be involved in anything like that. That is civilian police job, not ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke yesterday about your monthly sitrep about the shelling of the water queue in the eastern part of Sarajevo, did you personally check whether there was a front line nearby and how far was the water queue in relation to the positions of the warring parties in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I may have, but the information doesn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your mandate, did you know about the activities of the BH snipers within the part of town which was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did you go to any of the sniper -- so-called sniper nests in those parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have -- did you have any knowledge from which positions and from which buildings in the city of Sarajevo snipers of the BH army were active?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, not specific locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "No, not in specific locations," could you tell us, did you know more generally, in a wider sense, in which parts were the BH army snipers active?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniping was active, ma'am, virtually around the city on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Ierace, is there any need for re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked a question by my learned colleague as to whether you were able to determine the positions from which firing occurred onto the road and airport runway. You answered that question in relation to the road. Were you able to determine firing positions for the runway?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Today you were asked questions as to the meeting that you had with General Galic, that is, the meeting which was also attended by Mr. O'Keefe, and you said you would need to consult your diary in order to confirm the date of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P3448. In fact, I withdraw that. I think I have the only copy here, although it's marked, my copy is marked as a Prosecution Exhibit, we withdrew it at the last minute as a definite exhibit. So perhaps my copy can be shown to the witness. I indicate the Defence is being provided with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a receipt of the copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technical department will -- no, I don't have it on hand on one side, but on the other hand, I believe that Mr. Ierace could perhaps give us the B/C/S translation of this document. Then we would be certain that the General did receive it. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, a copy was disclosed to the Defence on the 26th of November, 2001. That information is contained in a letter that was sent to the Defence and copied to the Trial Chamber Bench, and there is not a B/C/S copy of the document. I am not sure whether my --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness doesn't look at this document until we have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, we wait, Mr. Carswell, to look at the document. I have no information that -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It may well be that this document was given to us in English, but I don't have it in Serbian and I don't think that General Galic could have seen it. I believe that this is a very voluminous document. That seems obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you know, the Chamber has drafted a form on which the Defence may indicate that there is not a translation available to them and it is an exhibit that has been indicated, and 3448 is indicated on the list in view of Mr. Carswell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it says it may not be tendered. That is what it says in the document. Consequently, I thought that these documents would not be handed over and so I did not see the translation in any case, Serbian translation, because it was never given to us. It was never offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I could assist by making clear that I do not intend to tender it. It is a document of the witness which I give him in order for him to refresh his memory. In other words, simply to check his contemporaneous note, that is, his diary, in order to determine the date of the meeting. There is no need to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just wanted to ask about the date of the meeting in order to take away any uncertainty about the memory of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, what I am surprised is that these pieces are produced not in the examination-in-chief, but in the sort of supplemental part. That is my first remark. The second remark is that General Galic would like us to confer, and that is his right, and I insist on this. Am I authorised to confer with his Excellency General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are always authorised to confer with your client, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. As far as the production or at least showing the document to the witness, it has been during cross-examination that it was stressed several times whether the recollection of the witness was precise as far as the date of the meeting was concerned, so it did not surprise me that much that the Prosecution would like to -- would like to avoid any misunderstandings. But please confer with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before I do it, would it be possible to do the following: To ask Mr. Ierace which is the page that he would like to show to the witness and then hand it to us and that so we can show it to General Galic and then confer with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have handed the witness the entire diary for him to check, but if my friend wishes it, I am happy, of course, to go to the relevant page. It is, of course, for the 24th of March. My friend will see there are two entries on that page, that is the 24th and the 25th of March and both of those, I anticipate, will be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then perhaps show to the Defence both of the relevant pages or the two entries on the specific page. Mr. Usher, could you please take the diary and bring it to Ms. Pilipovic and Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it will take half a minute. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It may happen that Ms. Pilipovic will have more questions on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is not tendered, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It will just be used for refreshing the memory of the witness, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And only as to the date, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my position is the following: This document, since it has not been translated into Serbian, and General Galic was not able to read it in his own language, it should not be submitted, shown to this witness, for a very simple reason, since that there are things in it on which there would be some questions that I could ask on behalf of General Galic and obviously we will not have time to do it during this hearing without the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, it will not be tendered. It will just be used to refresh the memory as far as the date of a meeting is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But it contains the period in question, the 24th. There are two pages of text and there are certain things regarding which the Defence would have questions to ask on behalf of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have had full opportunity, either to tender this document or to put whatever questions the Defence would have liked to put to the witness in respect of the entries in the document so this is not a moment to restart either the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination on other subjects. But let me just confer one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Mr. Ierace has indicated that he would use the document only for one question, which was repeatedly put to the witness during cross-examination, we will allow the witness to refresh his memory on the basis of this document. And, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you say you expected the document not to be tendered, first of all, it is not tendered by the Prosecution, but, secondly, if it says "it may not be tendered," that means that it is uncertain whether it will be tendered or not and you would not expect it on the basis of that indication, that it would not be tender said. But it will not be tendered, but the witness may use the -- his diary, at least the document, to refresh his memory. I take it that you opened the document on the very date or the dates that are relevant, so could please the document be presented to the witness. I think you would agree, Mr. Ierace, on that specific time period. Oh, it is closed again. Mr. Ierace, could you please find the page in the document which you think the witness would need to refresh his memory. Mr. Usher, could you please give the document to Mr. Ierace. Could you please locate the relevant page or pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. There is now a coloured marker on some of the letters. I expect that was done by the Defence. I have no problem with that. The document is open to the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it done by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am sorry. In the heat of the battle, I am really apologise, but this was done in the heat of the battle and we may have confused that document with ours. There was no malice, Mr. President. It was just -- we were trying to be swift about it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do notice that Mr. Ierace is grateful for the assistance you gave in this respect. Mr. Ierace, would you please open the document to that page and Mr. Usher, could you please show that page to the witness. Mr. Ierace, I take it that you now have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, would you look at the page in front of you and could you answer this question with just a yes or no. Firstly, are you able to determine from the diary the date of the meeting in question?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please give the date and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25 March.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might that be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that you said the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Finally, you are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please return the document to Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Finally you were asked questions yesterday and again today on the topic whether you carried out any investigation in relation to the discovery of gunpowder in oxygen bottles. Yesterday you said that you thought that it had been turned over to an investigative body and today you said you thought indeed it was CivPol. You have had read to you a passage from your entry for the 24th of January, 1993 in the monthly report which you drafted, do you -- withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be given P752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please hand over to the witness, P752.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you open that document at page 9 and look at the entry for the 24th of January. About halfway through that entries do these words appear: "Lima side UNMOs were called to the Blazuj hospital to witness that two of the oxygen bottles delivered by the UNHCR were found to contain gunpowder. Once confirmed, this matter was turned over to CivPol."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was CivPol?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian police, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please look at the entry for the 25th of January 1993 on the same page. Five lines from the bottom does this sentence appear: "The CivPol have take over the oxygen bottle investigation."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Carswell, Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Continuing with the CivPol, when you mentioned the CivPol, was the BH or the UN --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN CivPol, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yesterday, we had a lot of questions and answers on the issue of the random shooting.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And you said on page 32, line 23, that you personally saw no random shooting. You, personally, you didn't see random shootings. How do you know that there were random shootings? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not exactly sure of that discussion, sir, but when I say "I did not see random shooting," the way I would define that is I didn't see a gun fire a round and that round land in a marketplace or definitely not military target. I did see rounds landing, artillery rounds landing in areas that we would not expect to have seen, in other words, not on the front line. So when I say I didn't see something, I wasn't able to look you square in the eye and say I saw that gun fire that round which landed there, on a marketplace or some such. There certainly were rounds that were landing, it appeared, randomly, throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So you are -- idea is that there were random shootings --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most definitely. And when I talk about that, sir, I talk in the terms of artillery. In those days, when we did our ammunition counts, the hits in and outside of the city in the Serb lines and in the Bosnian lines, we do not count anti-aircraft fire or heavy machine-gun fire or rifle fire in that there was simply too much. We counted from 82 millimetre mortar up, therefore, very small artillery up to the larger weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to ask something to Ms. Pilipovic, clarification. And it is the following: Yesterday in one of your questions, you said that the "2nd, 6th and 3rd brigades, BH brigades, had Howitzers" but the document that you tendered yesterday, 108, doesn't mention a 6th Brigade. Was there a 6th Brigade or wasn't?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document I mentioned yesterday was the document of the 1st Corps. I spoke about the 6th Motorised Brigade which had a self-propelled artillery Howitzer battery, but I did not offer that document. I simply mentioned it to the witness. Self-propelled Howitzer battery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 6th Motorised Brigade did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like you to tell me about the precise sense or, rather, the exact meaning of the word "random." Do you mean that there was no method or without a conscious decision?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I had mentioned earlier, there were some mobile weapons, mortars, in particular, that we couldn't control, in that they were mobile and constantly on the move. I suspect - suspect - there may have been some random shooting, basically, putting a round either into the city or out of the city. And I -- the second part of your question, sir? I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exact meaning of the term that you used, of the word that you used.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. "Random," the way I would term it, with artillery, would be a round that would be fired with no real military value. Basically, the gun just lead into an area, in and on an area, and fired with -- without having identified anything specific in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, you are saying, if I understand you correctly, you are saying that "random" means that these were shots that were not targeting military targets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You said, and I am quoting in English, you said in relation to the shelling of the hospital, you said -- I believe that you said [In English] "Were under the impression it was a military target."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you come to that conclusion? If you allow me to explain my question. Did they follow orders coming from their superiors in the hierarchy saying that this was a military target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On my observations on the gun positions, when they were firing, it is easy to -- relatively easy to determine the sequence of events on a gun position. If I could use an example of one shoot, sir, the gunners were relaxing, having a cigarette, drinking coffee. The fire mission came down to the headquarters, to the battery headquarters, at which point they alerted the guns, did their plotting on the map, sent the information to the guns, and they fired. That was not random. I can't say that wasn't random, because I don't know the target. Obviously, I was well behind, out of sight. But the gunners on the guns in this particular case, in the number of cases that I saw, were controlled by their battery commander and I believe controlled by information that was passed down to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You spoke about the meeting that you had with Mr. -- with General Galic on the 25th of March. His reaction, could you perhaps inform us a little more about his reaction, because I believe that this was only about the attacks on the positions of the UN, not on the attacks on the targets in the city. Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions I asked, sir, I believe were -- my questions were dealing with targets on the OPs, on the UNMO positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and his reply, his response?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obviously cannot quote it verbatim. However, I remember, on the occasions that I spoke with him or his senior staff, the shelling of the OPs, of our OPs, the UN OPs, ceased for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So perhaps I have one last question for you: You spoke about knowing about the snipers that were members or part of the BH army. According to you, who were they targeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their targeting on the Serb side was much the same as the Serb targeting into the city. It appeared to be random. The father of my Serb interpreter, when I was working on the Lukavica side, was shot in his backyard. However, being a professional soldier, sir, I really do object to the term "sniper," and I do know that is common usage. It was random shooting going back and forth, and it seemed to me that virtually everything was fair game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well, Mr. Carswell. You were talking about targeting a hospital and you mentioned Kosevo hospital. Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, no, although that is -- I know it is in my sitreps. That was generally -- generally very important in that CNN seemed to get there before any of us. Almost on a daily basis, sir, but I can't -- in and around, but I can't, without looking at my sitreps, pin it down, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we would have the sitreps, we could find out. That is during your stay?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNMO sitreps would be much, much more illuminating than this document, which is simply excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You talked about Kosevo hospital as a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information that the Kosevo hospital grounds be used by the ABiH forces to fire from?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many occasions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Many occasions. If you are saying "many," is that 5, 50, 500?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is 25 or more, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 25, yes. Yesterday, you used the expression when asked about the means of communication: "Motorola." I know that is a make, but what exactly were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A short range set, hand-held wireless set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us that, to your knowledge, fuses of - I think it was mortars - was set in such a way that they would explode at a height of 20 or 30 metres so that there would be a shower of shrapnel. Was this the usual way, in your experience, these projectiles were used?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mortars, they were anti-aircraft guns. They were light anti-aircraft, probably from anywhere to 20 to 40 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would not be similar as far as mortars are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that, according to your knowledge, that the Bosnian Serb forces were quite accurate in their targeting. You also told us that from their positions, with two exceptions, they could not see their targets.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to us on what basis you could testify that they were accurate in their targeting, but could not see their targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Three things: The first, when I checked the mechanism of the guns and had a look at them, there was allowable play, very little play in the mechanisms when I moved the barrels, which told me that that gun, once laid with -- properly, would probably fire where it was supposed to, according to the data that was given to the gun crew. The second was the professionalism of the command post. The command post crew were, as I mentioned, probably manned by ex-JNA and they were good at their work. They were very efficient. The third point, and most telling, is that the guns did not move, therefore, the first few missions they fired into town would probably have a lot of adjustment to do to get the rounds to drop. Usually, it takes sometimes up to five rounds. You are lucky if you hit one with three. You can be close at three, but you're lucky if you hit. With five rounds, you can definitely do well. Those guns never moved. I suspect a lot of the targets that came down were the same. So they knew virtually exactly where the rounds would land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well, it is your testimony that all the circumstances were there for very accurate targeting, which is not the same as accurate targeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the preregistered targets, the targets that they had fired before, if the guns had fired those targets before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They could have accurately --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be very accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you saw sniper rifles from a distance at the Bosnian Serb side. Could you tell us under what circumstances you saw them? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were being moved, sir. A sniper does not advertise his profession or his location. And I saw them on both sides, on the Bosnian side and on the Serb side. I didn't see many but I saw some. The object of a sniper is to be able to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is under what circumstances did you see it? I mean, people carrying sniper rifles or being stored in apartment block building or --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: People moving them from one location or to another. Either to a vehicle -- either to a vehicle or to a building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means not in use, not in storage, but being taken from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us about your meetings with General Galic. You also told us that there was an interpreter there. Did you observe any fact which would indicate that General Galic would understand the English language as well? Or did you ever hear him to speak in words of English?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard the general speak in English. It was my impression that there was some understanding of English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what basis did you get this impression?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: By people-watching, sir. When you make a comment, it is standard, before when you make a standard, before it goes through the interpreter, to watch the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the questions that was asked to you, and I just like to clarify whether your answer was specifically to that question. The question was as it reads in the transcript: "During your mandate, did you know about activities of the BH snipings, I think it was, within the part of town which was under the control of the BH army?" Did you understand this question on which you answer was: "yes, madam." Did you understand this question to be about sniping within the part of town that both firing and receiving the fire was within that part of the town; or did you understand the question as relate to firing from within the town, which is not the same, because then the fire could be received out of that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, sir, was firing from the Bosnian side to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Within. . .

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From within the city to Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Yes, these were my questions. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a clarification following the questions asked by the Chamber, I just wanted to clarify one point f you will allow me, it is just one point to clarify. But it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question of the Chamber, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will speak to you in French. First of all, good afternoon. You answered a question by the Chamber and it was whether the shelling could have been considered as very precise and you answered "yes." And I am indicating that this is page 25, line 10. And you answered you said, you replied in the affirmative, you said what you said "if the guns had fired to those on those targets before." Could you, Witness, if that is the case, confirm to us that with the expression "guns" you were meaning the cannons, rather than mortars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been both, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Witness, that a mortar is much more mobile than a cannon, and therefore, your explanation about the stability of heavy artillery like cannons, would not be applicable to mortars?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to what you said about the stability of the canners, can you confirm to the Chamber that this is the case, that any cannon has a has a hitback mechanism, and that this hitback mechanism, a recoil mechanism could move the cannon by itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, therefore, after a certain number of hits that means that the target, the site, has to be adjusted after several hits were fired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is adjusted after every round is fired, sir

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Ierace, that this does not raise any need for further examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it does, but I again, I am very conscious of time constraints. There will be an artillery expert. I will wait until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming and answering the questions of both parties and the Bench. It is important for us to hear answers from witnesses for the task that we will have to fulfill. Thank you very much for coming. And would you please, Mr. Usher, escort Mr. Carswell out of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before Mr. Mundis calls the next witness, I would like to raise the issue of timetable. I note that Mr. Carswell has left the Trial Chamber one hour beyond the time which would have been taken if cross-examination and other issues had been confined to double that which the Prosecution took in chief. Please, understand Mr. President, I am in no way being critical, of course, of questioning of the Bench, far from it. Mr. President what I am concerned about is the issue of the Defence interjecting with objections which consume much time, and which on many occasions, in my respectful submission were rather unnecessary or avoidable. In particular, Mr. Piletta-Zanin consumed some minutes at least in stating to the Trial Chamber that he did not have an opportunity in effect, to -- at least the Defence did not have an opportunity -- to cross-examine Mr. Carswell on the contents of his diary. I drew to the attention of the Trial Chamber that a copy was disclosed to the Defence for the first time on the 26th of November last year. Now, it was disclosed after that and perhaps Mr. Piletta-Zanin will be reminded by me saying this, that last Thursday, the 9th of May, he met with a member of the Prosecution legal trial team, Stefan Waespi, who handed him a copy of the diary, 200 pages in English and Mr. Piletta-Zanin said that he wanted it for his trip to Zurich. They then discussed whether a B/C/S translation was required. Now, perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin now remembers that. My basic point is this: That if the Prosecution is to have any hope of reaching the target, the matters which are beyond its control and are not necessary, perhaps could be confined to a minimum. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. The Chamber has taken notice of your observation. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to enter further into this subject, moreover because I never travelled to Zurich. But before another witness comes into the Chamber, and to speak of things that are infinitely more serious, the Defence heard the evidence as formulated by the witness, that a very important fact came to light and that was that military equipment of first class equipment material, gunpowder for cannons was transported in a secret way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are now commenting on the evidence. In due course you will be in a position, so will you please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, I am coming to the point which is the following: The evidence came to light that UN civilian services carried out an investigation on this point. Now in application of the Rule 71 of the Rules, Mr. President, it is within the authority of your Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do understand that you in one way or the other want to introduce evidence in relation to that investigation. Did you ask the Prosecution whether they had anything available and did you consider then to, while presenting your case, to tender that evidence? I first want you to communicate with the Prosecution rather than starting raising issues in this court which have not been discussed before. If the discussions would result in nothing or if there are serious reasons to bring the matter to the attention of the Chamber, we will hear the observations, but not until you have discussed the matter with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will come back to it tomorrow, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or the day after tomorrow, depends on when you will have an opportunity to meet with the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I be excused, Mr. President? I don't think there are any exhibits in relation to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. Carswell, we will still have 698, I think 752, and 816, if I am correct. Madam Registrar, could you confirm that. And that would be -- 698 would be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respectfully interrupt. Two matters. First of all, there is the issue of confidentiality, in relation to the documents, but secondly, the manner in which I referred the witness to those documents, the various documents, I think negates the need to tender them and is respectful of your express desire yesterday that the tendered documents be kept to an absolute minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be as well as for 752?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the January report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we had D108, which was not tendered by the Defence finally, if I do understand well. Just be shown to the witness, he said he didn't know the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on which we have to take any decisions. Mr. Mundis, your next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution calls Jeremy Peter Hermer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom. May I use the short break to stress again that the Defence has to remain within the time limits of the examination-in-chief, which was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put on the headphones in case someone might use another language and the witness doesn't understand. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are speaking English. Mr. Hermer, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher and may I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hermer. Please be seated. Could you please come close to the microphone and, Mr. Usher, do I see well that one of the microphones is off? Yes, both on. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you already in advance to find a suitable moment for a break in up to 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hermer, you are currently a major in the Royal Marines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long have you been in the Royal Marines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I have been serving with the Royal Marines now since 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The summer of 1993, were you posted as an UNMO in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you commence that duty?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I commenced as an UNMO in late July 1993. I moved from sector south in to Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 23rd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were you assigned upon arrival in Bosnia in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was assigned to Sarajevo to the -- what was known as the Lima side, the Lima team working on the Serb side of the front line in Sarajevo out of Lukavica barracks. I was then sent immediately on to Mount Igman with a team that was operating in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you arrive on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Pretty much as soon as I arrived in the Sarajevo area and that is where I continued to work from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So that would be approximately 23 August 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Approximately then. One or two days for administration when I first arrived in Sarajevo, and then straight up onto the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were your duties on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My duties were initially to oversee an implementation of an agreement which had been reached between UNPROFOR and the warring factions to withdraw forces from the area of Mount Igman. I was required to liaise with local commanders, to ensure that the withdrawals had taken place in accordance with that agreement. That meant moving extensively around the area, liaising with Bosnian commanders, Serbian commanders and assuring that no infiltration of the area was taking place by either warring party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long were you posted on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I remained on Mount Igman from late August until mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were you then posted?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was then withdrawn from Mount Igman down to Lukavica barracks which was the Lima side headquarters and I was then moved from one observation post to another. I can't remember how many I visited on the Lima side for approximately a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than visiting the Lima OPs during this week period, what did you do while you were in Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was working as an UNMO on the Lima side, working in and around the headquarters, assisting in various duties. And basically travelling around, as I said, from one OP to another getting to know the ground, getting to know the area on the Serb side and also meeting with a few local commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After this approximate one-week period of being at Lukavica and the Lima OPs, where were you then posted?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was then sent into Sarajevo to the military observers, the UNMOs' headquarters in the PTT building and I was assigned the task of MIO, military information officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date that you arrive for duty at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Approximately 12, 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you remain posted at the PTT building for the duration of your tour as an UNMO in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I stayed, my main post was within the PTT building in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the UNMOs' headquarters, the operations room until the remainder of my tour until January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this period -- during this period, did you also primarily or were you primarily quartered in the PTT building as well?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, throughout I was quartered in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were your primary duties as military information officer or MIO?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My primary duties were to collate information which was coming in to the headquarters from a number of sources. Those sources would be the other military observers in the various OPs. Information received by satellite communications, information from local commanders and information from the other UN battalion MIOs. Once we have collated, my responsibility was as far as possible to analyse that, to extract it, and then once daily to assist in the compilation of the sector situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Among the sources that you relied on, did you rely on incident reports from the various Papa and Lima observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The vast majority of information coming in to the operations room was real-time information, which was coming in on a minute-by-minute basis on the VHF radio frequency net. That information was coming in as it happened on the ground. It was reported to me in the Ops room and I would then note that in the incident log and obviously that would go towards the situation report at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These records were referred to as "incident reports" or IncReps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also rely upon daily sitreps coming from the Papa headquarters and from the Lima headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That's correct. Both sides, both Lima and Papa would compile their own situation reports, which would be with me by mid to late afternoon. I would use those to form a basis of my own situation report which would then get pushed up to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "headquarters" do you mean the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, primarily our reports went to the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb. It was also passed, that information, on to Kiseljak, to Geneva and to New York, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of information would be included in the IncReps coming from the OPs?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: What would normally happen if I can just take you through a sequence of events, if I may, on the ground. There would be an incident on the ground, say, for example, a shell would land. If a Papa side observation post saw that landing, they would report an IncRep, so immediately it occurred, they'd report a date, a time, and as near as possible a location for that incident, and then they would describe it as best as possible, incoming fire, outgoing fire, whatever it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, do you have any idea why you were assigned to be the person collating and collecting this information?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was assigned into the that location, to the best of my knowledge, because I was a native English speaker. There was a vast amount of information to be processed in realtime. There was a distinct advantage to being a native English speaker and that is why I found myself in the headquarters able to deal rapidly with information, process it and to report and communicate effectively in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The sitreps, the outgoing sitreps were done in English is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That were done in English, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time you were stationed as an UNMO in Bosnia, you were a junior captain, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: A very junior captain, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President this would be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. We will have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you may resume the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, prior to the break you were telling us about incident reports that you received from both the Papa side and the Lima side. Can you give the Trial Chamber a ballpark figure as to the breakdown of the specific incident reports that you received from each side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: In terms of a ratio?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The ratio of incident reports was quite largely biased towards those reports coming from the Papa side. I -- that is, incidents occurring on the Bosnian side of the confrontation line. As a ratio, I would say that we would receive approximately 100 incident reports on the Papa side for 1 or 2 occurring on the Lima side. You need to bear in mind that these reports weren't just incoming rounds, they were outgoing rounds as well. So, for example, if a gun were firing on the Lima side on the Serb side, that would also be reported as an incident report. But the vast majority of reports were explosions or incoming rounds or sniper activity, on the Bosnian side, because those things, by their very nature, are easier to see and witness than weapons firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "on the Bosnian side" do you mean that the Bosnian side was, for lack of a better term, the recipient of that shelling and sniping activity?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, unlike the situation reports, incident reports would only be generated when something happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. They were reported realtime as a result of an action taking place on the ground, physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the basis of these numerous incident reports that you received from the Papa side, were you able to draw any overall conclusions about events that were happening on the Bosnian side, on the inside of the Bosnian lines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was quite easy to draw conclusions from the evidence that we were witnessing, on a minute-by-minute basis. The conclusions which I think we all drew, certainly which I drew, were that there was a vast amount of ordinance or ammunition landing on the Bosnian side of the confrontation, i.e., in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the incident reports that you received contain information as to what were the objects of this incoming fire?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: They would. Initially, of course it wasn't always obvious to the observer. Sometimes, of course, it was. However, where possible, they would give an indication of what they thought the intended target was or otherwise, be it a legitimate military target, or a random round landing in a residential area, for example, with no obvious military target at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, do you have any specific recollection as to the approximate breakdown of the incident reports that you receive concerning legitimate military targets or as you put it "random rounds"? Do you have any recollection of the breakdown of those two categories?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It would be very difficult to give you a breakdown. There were times when there were obvious military actions taking place, when there was sustained fire coming into the city, around the front lines that was obviously directed at military-type targets. But for the majority of the time, i.e., throughout a 24-hour period, there would be continual background activity if you like, of ammunition, small arms fire, heavy weapons fire, shelling, which would be landing seemingly randomly throughout the Sarajevo area, inside the city. It was almost impossible to say with any conviction that the majority of this activity was directed at any specific military target because in the majority of cases, wherever the ammunition was landing, there was no military target present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon receipt of these incident reports, did you or any of the other UN personnel in the PTT building, or on the ground, attempt to locate the source of the fire, whether it was artillery or sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Where possible, we would always try to locate the source of the fire. Occasionally, I say occasionally, some of the time, an incoming incident report on the Bosnian side reported by a Papa OP, would also correspond directly with an outgoing, i.e., a firing incident report, reported by a Lima OP on the Serbian side of the line. It was, therefore, relatively easy to draw a correlation between the two, and to come to the conclusion that the two were linked, i.e., the gun that had been witnessed firing was responsible for the round that we saw landing, but that didn't always happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the event there was no direct evidence of this type of firing and impacting, were you nonetheless able to reach any type of conclusions, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, we were. Through experience, really, time served in the city, we were able to make judgments as to which gunlines, or gun positions or front line positions, various impacts or sniping was coming from. Quite apart from that, after the incident had taken place, it was possible, certainly with cases of indirect fire, mortar fire or shell fire, to carry out a crater analysis which would given an indication as to the range and direction of the firing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently were crater analyses undertaken?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The vast majority of incidents were not analysed in any way, only those which were noteworthy or significant in terms of the impact or the effect they caused. For example, if a significant number of civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why were crater analyses not conducted routinely?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: They were simply not the manpower, the available expertise or the time to deal with every incident that occurred. We are talking on some days many hundred of independent shell impacts. It would not be possible to carry out detailed analysis of those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And all of the incidents that you are talking about occurred on the Bosnian side of the line, that is, these crater impacts, these shellings that you are describing right now, occurred on the Bosnian-controlled side of the line?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No, no. There were impacts indeed on the Serb side of the line as well. There were markedly less, far fewer, but there were incidents of rounds landing on the Serbian side too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were assigned to the Lukavica barracks and you travelled from OP to OP, did you have the opportunity to visit any VRS gun positions around the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Both to the south of the city, along the Pale road area, to the west of the city, Vogosca area and its environs, and to the north of the city as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will ask you more specific questions about those sites later, but for now I have just a couple of questions. First, with respect to those artillery positions that you saw to the south of the city, was there -- excuse me, was there also a Lima OP in the general vicinity of those gun locations to the south?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Wherever possible, the Lima headquarters would attempt to place its Lima OP in the near vicinity of a gun position or gun positions. This wasn't always possible for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate, please.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The -- although the vast majority of the gun positions were fixed, there was or the Serbs retained the ability to move their guns fairly rapidly, which would obviously be done without us receiving any prior warning. There were also restrictions put upon our movement, on the Serb side of the line. These restrictions would sometimes be more severe than other times they would be increased and decreased without warning. And as the UNMOs in HOP were generally required to accommodate themselves there as well, we were limited in our choice of location because the OP had to give not only good fields of view and access to gun positions, but also had to accommodate the team that occupied the OP. We were also obliged to put a request in through the Lukavica barracks headquarters for increase in OPs and for accommodation and that wouldn't always necessarily be met with approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You testified a few moments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I was waiting for the end of the sentence of the witness. When witnesses is answering far too quickly and I have seen or heard rather some difficulties in the French interpretation. I did not intervene in order not to stop the rhythm, but if the witness could be asked to speak more slowly

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hermer, you heard the observation. Can you please slow down in your answer, everything has to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, a few moments ago you told us that the Lima OPs would submit incident reports if they were aware of firing from the Bosnian Serb army gun positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have also testified that on some days there were hundreds of shells landing in the city of Sarajevo; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain in light of your answer that there were Lima OPs near gun positions to the maximum extent possible, why there weren't more incident reports of outgoing VRS artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Well, there are probably a number of reasons why that would be the case. Firstly, the nature of gunfire, when it is coming from the gun position, in terms of sound, et cetera is far less easy to detect than impacting ammunition, i.e., an explosion. If atmospheric conditions are wrong, then it is possible that a gun position could be firing its guns only a few hundred metres away and you wouldn't be able to detect that. The Lima side of the front line was quite extended. I forget now how many kilometres were being covered, but there were very few teams to cover that and there were a great number of gun positions that we were responsible for covering. That problem of not being able to detect the guns firing or mortar firing was sometimes exacerbated by the fact that during intense periods of activity, we would have a blanket movement restriction placed upon us on the Lima side. So our UNMOs would not be able to travel around and observe the gun positions, as they would wish to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
