utterances.text: During the time that you were in Sarajevo do you recall approximately how many Lima OPs were functioning?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: In total, my recollection is that we had up to 12 OPs, but there were times when, due to manpower shortages, or indeed restrictions placed upon us, we had to close OPs down. So the maximum number that I recall is 12, although we were frequently operating with less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, during the time that you were assigned as an MIO in Sarajevo, did you have any responsibilities with respect to communicating with the VRS liaison officers at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Both as the MIO, and then later in my tour as I became the operations officer, I had responsibilities for, wherever possible, communicating with the Serbian liaison officer, officer, based in Lukavica. And that would be carried out as and when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you recall the name of the Serbian liaison officer at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The Serbian liaison officer with whom I had most contact was one Major Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever personally meet Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, I met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the first time that you met with him, approximately when that was, and where?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The first time I met Major Indjic, I believe, was early in my time in Sarajevo when I was first deployed up on to Mount Igman. I believe that I met him, if not on my first day, then possibly my second day, at Lukavica when he was introduced to me as the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did anyone explain to you what his role was as the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No. His role was never clearly explained to me. I made the assumption, I guess, that he would have the duties of any liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: And based on your military experience, what were the responsibilities of the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: To my knowledge, and having been a liaison officer myself, responsibilities are to build relationships with the factions concerned, or the elements concerned, and with personalities and to facilitate a transferral of information backwards and forwards, and really that's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which unit or military organisation Major Indjic was attached to?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was never clearly stated. And again, I believe, at the time I made the assumption that he was, in fact, working for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: As his permanent place of residence, or rather his permanent place of work, was Lukavica barracks, and as time progressed, it became evident to me that he was able to somehow influence, or have an affect on what was occurring with the fighting troops on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will go into that in slightly greater detail in few moments. But let me ask you this: When you were stationed in the PTT building, did you have regular interaction with Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My answer is: Yes, either directly or indirectly, I had regular contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Through what means was that contact established?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There were a number of ways in which our paths crossed. Firstly, I would meet him occasionally in the Lukavica headquarters itself, where he was often in and around the military observers or the UNMO operations room. I would have access to him or to his office via a fixed landline communication link, which I would use to contact either the Lima UNMO Ops room or indeed to talk to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In civilian a fixed landline communication link would be a telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently would you speak with Major Indjic on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to remember how frequently I spoke to him. My recollection is that I had a number of telephone conversations directly with that individual, however, if I wasn't able to speak to him directly, then my messages or requests or complaints would be passed directly to him by one of the Lima military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In what language did you communicate with Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And based on your discussions with him, was it clear to you that he understood English?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On those occasions when you spoke with him on the telephone, did you dial his number directly, or did you dial a different number?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My recollection of that is poor. I am unable to remember whether I had a specific telephone number for his office or whether I only had the one number that would link me to the military observers. What I do recall is that it was possible to get him on the end of the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Lima operations room at Lukavica barracks, do you recall in which building that centre was located?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That was in the -- the only building which I had access to, which was the largest building directly inside the main gates on the right-hand side, which I understood to be the main headquarters building of Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the Sarajevo Romanija Corps head quartered in that building?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there were elements of headquarters staff working from that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was Major Indjic's office in relation to the Lima Ops office?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I am not aware of where his office was, specifically. Again, my recollection is not good of that particular question, but I am inclined to believe that it was located on the first floor somewhere near the UNMOs Ops room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge or information about the location of General Galic's office?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During any time when you were at Lukavica barracks, did you have any discussion with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever encounter or meet General Galic in that building?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I encountered General Galic on, to my knowledge, possibly, two occasions. On one occasion, he was very very briefly introduced to me, in passing, and on the other occasion, we just happened to be in the same area at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On those occasions when you picked up the telephone and dialed the number for Lukavica barracks, whom were you intending to speak to on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Normally, it was my intention to speak to the Lima UNMOs, either the Lima duty officer, whoever that might have been on the day, or the Lima team commander who was, at that time, a Danish officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many times, during the five-month period that you were either the MIO or the Ops officer at the PTT building, did you phone the Lima OPs centre at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Again I could not realistically put a figure on that, not even an approximate one. But if you consider that I was in the operations room in the PTT building for essentially five months, and depending on the severity of the actions taking place in town, and the level of activity, the number of phone calls I would make would range from none to five or six in a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall periods -- you have said "none in a day." Do you recall periods where there would be several days that would elapse between days of a phone call?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There were certainly quiet periods when there was no reason to telephone. I actually want to rephrase that. The telephone line was used regularly, but for administrative purposes a lot of the time. I would use that line to speak to the Lima headquarters, if necessary, to carry out routine conversations. What I said previously about not using the line at all, was with regard to making specific complaints or requests, based upon the military action going on in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of complaints or specific requests would you be making when you called Lukavica barracks? Can you give a few concrete examples?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I can give you some -- I can give you some generic examples, certainly. If there was activity happening in the city, it may well occur that a Bosnian local commander would lodge a complaint through the Papa UNMO headquarters team. The complaint could be that there was extensive shelling, for example, or sniping in one particular area that was not directed at any specific military target, and possibly that civilians were being injured. That complaint would be passed to me, either via VHF radio or by telephone, in the PTT building and I would then, if I thought it necessary, contact the Lima headquarters to pass on my concern or to ask for an explanation of the activity that was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than complaints lodged by local Bosnian commanders, was there any other source of the complaints that you would then pass on to Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes. The military observers themselves may well place a request or a complaint. For example, on a number of occasions we had shells landing very close to our OPs, within metres in fact. Or we had our patrolling team, who were being engaged by snipers. I would receive a message to that effect and, of course, would then contact Lima headquarters to try to ascertain why that was occurring and to request that it be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I am going to focus now your attention on the phone calls concerning complaints that you lodged with Lukavica barracks. In order to clarify your earlier answer, there were some days when you made no such phone calls, and on other days you called, I believe you said, five or six times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It varied, depending upon what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the phone calls concerning complaints, do you have any idea how many times you spoke to Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Again, I couldn't give you a specific figure of the number of times we spoke. Again, I refer back to the explanation I gave earlier. Over a five-month period, there were times when I would speak to him regularly, sometimes, as I say, directly; maybe five and six times in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there other occasions when you would speak with one of the Lima duty Ops officers when it was clear to you that Major Indjic was in the room?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were times when it was obvious to me or it seemed obvious to me on my end of the telephone line that the operations officer on the Lima side or the duty officer were having a conversation directly with a Serb liaison officer. And out of experience, I would have guessed that that would be Major Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On those occasions when you spoke directly with Major Indjic, with respect to complaints about shelling or sniping what type of responses did you receive from Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There were a number of types of response one could expect to receive. And they ranged from total indifference and unwillingness to communicate to a denial, a flat denial of any action taking place. It may well be that he would be aware of what I was referring to and his retort was that this was legitimate military action and a response to earlier Bosnian actions. On occasion he would, again, appear to be aware of to what I was referring and would, in fact, say that he would try to do something positive to help the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience did Major Indjic do anything "positive" to help the situation?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It certainly appeared to me and to a number of my colleagues that at times, Major Indjic seemed to be able to cause an effect on the battlefield, if you like, in that when a request or complaint had been lodged, the incident to which the complaint referred often ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know it ceased?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Sometimes difficult to tell whether or not it had ceased as a result of Major Indjic's intervention or whether it had naturally abated. But a pattern emerged eventually, whereby it would be difficult to say that it was pure coincidence that when these complaints or requests were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. lodged. The specific request that we had placed happened within a short time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on this pattern, whereby you would make a specific request and shortly thereafter the conduct of which you were complaints would cease, did you draw any conclusion about the effectiveness of contacting Lukavica barracks to lodge a complaint?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There was always the possibility that contacting Lukavica barracks would elicit some kind of positive action. Therefore, I was dutybound always to make that contact in the hope that something positive could -- could happen. As I said previously, it wasn't always the case. But on the occasions where either Major Indjic, directly or through one of my colleagues on the Lima side, indicated something could happen then generally something did appear to happen. So I would say that there was a chance that something would happen when a request was lodged and, therefore, there was the possibility that our request would be granted, which leads me to believe that Major Indjic, or somebody in that headquarters, had the ability to cause an effect on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently, when you made these calls, did they result in a positive outcome or a positive result?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Not as frequently as one would have hoped. On the occasions when there was a positive response, and a positive effect caused then those occasions became quite significant, especially in my memory. It wasn't unusual and it was possible to put pressure on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Well, I know on a couple of occasions when, I think, on one particular occasion, there was some severe sniping taking place, we had lodged a complaint by telephone to the headquarters in Lima and Major Indjic had come on the line. On that particular occasion, I recall that he was denying anything was happening. I have to confess at that time to fabricating a story and telling him there was a CNN newsteam on the ground filming it, to which I recall his response was "I will get back to you. I will see what I can do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did he, in fact, get back to you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did he tell you when he got back in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The details of the specific conversation are not very clear, but the effect was that something would be done and that there was a legitimate reason for the sniping taking place however, it would stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any confirmation that the sniping did, in fact, stop?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience in the military, did you draw any conclusions about Major Indjic's area of responsibility or his duties within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: You mean personal conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was, I think, somewhat surprised by the level of influence that Major Indjic appeared to have on what was happening at the front line. On many occasions, when asked to do something about the situation, when he agreed that, in fact, he would, he intimated or indicated by his manner and tone that it was him directly that was having this effect, by talking to commanders. I don't know whether that is the case or not or whether in fact he would have gone to the operations staff and spoken to them, I don't know. But it seemed to me that on many occasions, he was able to make almost independent -- or take independent decisions. Usually, with regard to what was happening in terms of the conflict. I was also required to speak to him regularly to try to facilitate clearances and freedom of movement agreements. In those case where he was obviously dealing with policy pertaining to UNPROFOR, he would never make a decision. He would always refer it up to his high command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there instances when you lodged complaints, with respect to shelling or sniping, where Major Indjic intimated to you that he was going to speak to his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Well, he would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question seems very leading, since it contains the answer in itself. It should not be phrased in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there instances, other than the instance in which you have said, Major Indjic told you that he would get back to you, were there other instances where Major Indjic informed you that he would call you back?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was going to call you back?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Generally, he would sometimes he would indicate that he was, indeed, going to find out the facts, really, for want of a better word, better explanation. I could be wrong, but I don't specifically recall him using the need or citing the need to consult with the chain of command as a reason for delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your, again, experience in the British military, would you characterise the chain of command within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps as being one that was relatively tight and rigid or one that was relatively loose?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I believe there to be a tight chain of command within Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There were obviously professional officers working in that organisation who were able to maintain that rigid military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Based on 17 years of military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions now concerning incidents of sniping. During the period of time when you were stationed and billeted in Sarajevo, did you personally witness any events of sniping?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I did frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall a specific incidence near the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it. Would you like me to take you through that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could, and first of all tell us the approximate time period in which that incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was in October of 1993, the exact date and time, I am not able to recall. But it was a significant event for me inasmuch as I was under sniper fire myself. I was travelling in my light military vehicle in eastern Sarajevo, the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt briefly. What do you mean by a "light military vehicle"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: A civilian-style four-wheel drive. The vehicle, in this case, a Toyota Landcruiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What colour was the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was painted white and it was carrying the full United Nations insignia, along with other decals which indicated in Serbo-Croat that it contained unarmed military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I heard one of our teams, one of our Papa teams, who were, at that time, responding to some heavy sniping that was going on in and around the area of the Holiday Inn. The team, as I recall, indicated that there was a significant amount of sniping and that at that time two people had been killed, two civilians had been killed. One was a pregnant woman. And that team, the Papa 1 team had moved to that location to observe what was happening. I was only a matter of a few hundred metres away from that incident and decided to go and assist. As I arrived at the Holiday Inn, my vehicle came under fire from small arms and I was able to put my vehicle behind a large concrete block which protected it from the fire, as the fire was coming from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know an approximate location or building from which the fire was coming?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was between 400 and 500 metres away. To the south there was a block of flats. There appeared to be more than one sniper in that building and we could, in fact, observe a muzzled flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall on which side of the confrontation line the sniper or snipers was located?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: According to our knowledge at the time and the mapping that we had and our experience, that building was, in fact, on the Serb side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: What -- the scene that I witnessed when I arrived is that there were a number of civilians in that area who the evidently been going about their normal daily business, when the sniping had started and were essentially, therefore, for want of a better phrase, "pinned down" and unable to move as every time somebody tried to move in that area then they were engaged by the snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many civilians were in this cluster of people?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Number. It is difficult to recall because people were taking -- people were taking cover and people were bunched together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than yourself in the white UN vehicle, did you see any significant military presence of the ABiH in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: At that time when I was there, there was none and as I understood it, there had been none previously either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain at this location?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Less than half an hour. We did contact the headquarters in the PTT building, asked them to report this to the Lima side, what was occurring, to try to cause some effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if, in fact, the Lima side was contacted and what, if any, effect did this contact have?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The Lima side was contacted, as I remember. Ultimately people were able to move from that location, i.e., the snipers ceased their engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to another incident involving sniping that you witnessed long sniper alley near the government buildings; do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That incident was later. It was in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not certain about this, but I don't think I heard this witness speak about Sniper Alley as such. Could perhaps Mr. Mundis tell us where he referred to it. I mean, page and line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can elicit that from the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also, Mr. President, I apologise but I have two sets of headphones and one of them is very uncomfortable, because I would like to have the ability to follow the French booth as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you are able to solve the problem on your own, we would not have had to spend a minute on it. Of course I am willing to assist you, if necessary, but finally you solved the problem and the pause was not necessary at all. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, do you recall give a statement from an investigator of the Tribunal in June of 2001?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in your statement did you make reference to Sniper Alley?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I think that is very likely. The answer is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was that a term that you came to be aware of during the time you lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was a term which was synonymous with Sarajevo and it referred to an area in the city which was particularly prone to sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what area of the city that term refers to?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It refers to the main thoroughfare running from east to west into the Old City or Stari Grad, particularly from the area of the Holiday Inn towards the government buildings and along the river. It also encompassed an area known as Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to an incident in which you were travelling along Sniper Alley near the government buildings and you witnessed some sniping activity. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was snow on the ground at the time. It was early December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what you witnessed on that occasion, please.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I was driving from east to west, having just visited the Papa UNMO headquarters, and I was in the vehicle with one other military observer. We were driving a white, United Nations marked, GMC truck, which was the only armoured vehicle that we had, within the UNMO team. As we were driving just past the government buildings heading from east to west, to our front, some 15, 20 metres in front of us, there were three large strikes, ammunition strikes or ordinance strikes on the road to our front. Simultaneously with this, I noticed a change in the mannerism of the large number of civilians who were also in that area. It was a phenomenon which I experienced regularly in Sarajevo and I liken it to the way a flock of -- rather a school of fish will change direction all at once, without any prior warning. As the rounds hit the ground in front of us, the crowd which consisted of I don't know between 20 and 50 people. Simultaneously, lowered their bodies and ducked their heads and moved into cover. Everyone did this simultaneously. It was if it was a well-rehearsed drill. From my first observations, the fact that there were three rounds landing almost simultaneously and the size of the impact, I assessed that this was, in fact, a heavy-calibre weapon which was being fired into the road. The only possible targets in that area were the civilians, the road and my vehicle. So, myself and my colleague, again, put the vehicle into cover, got out of the vehicle, in cover, and observed the road to our front. Within a few seconds, there was more firing and what had happened effectively was that the crowd of people who had been moving from east to west across the road were now stuck either side of that road. I remember clearly that there was one mother with her child who was separated on one side of the road from her child who was on our side of the road. What had happened at that stage was that because the gun that was firing had a clear line of sight all the way down this road, this effectively split the city, at that point, into east and west. And any transit across that road was potentially lethal. We remained in that area for approximately 15 minutes, I would say, throughout which time a number of people were brave enough to cross the road. Each time somebody emerged from cover and tried to cross the road, another burst of automatic heavy machine-gun fire would come down crashing down in front of us. When nobody was moving, the gun wasn't firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any of these civilians crossing the road struck by gunfire on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have characterised the impacting rounds as being large calibre machine-gun fire. Do you have any knowledge about what calibre you believed those rounds to be?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It is impossible to tell specifically at the point of impact the calibre of a weapon, but, based on experience both in the UK and particularly in Sarajevo, I made the assessment that it was at least 12.7 millimetre heavy machine-gun fire and that was characterised by the size of the impacts and indeed the sound of the gun firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the location of the gunner on that instance?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was quite easy to assess the time between impact and hearing the gunfire -- through calculating the time between impact and hearing the gunfire that the position was quite a few hundred metres off to our south. What was actually happening was that the rounds were hitting the ground in front of us before we heard the gun firing because the sound was taking quite some time to travel that distance. And, indeed, the rounds were travelling faster than sound. So that, combined with the angle from which the ammunition was coming, led us to assess that the gun was being fired from up on the hill from the Serb-held positions just below the road to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, were there instances when you were on the Bosnian Serb army side of the line and you witnessed weapons being fired?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons did you witness being fired?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I witnessed all manner of weapons being fired, but over the period of my tenure in Sarajevo however, the majority of them were what I will term "indirect fire weapons", artillery or mortar pieces, and it wasn't always possible to see where those weapons were aimed and where the rounds were landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you ever recall seeing any anti-aircraft artillery weapons along the Bosnian Serb army side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of weapons that were specifically designed to be used in the anti-aircraft role, which were being used in the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are standing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes I have to do it. I am sorry. In the French transcript, we may have an error and it is important to underline this. We are talking about the Serb confrontation line. I do not think that there were Serb or Muslim confrontation lines. So I think it would be necessary to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we have the small yellow papers for these minor things. It took, again, a minute. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, you were talking about triple-A guns, that is, anti-aircraft artillery guns, and I believe the point when you were interrupted you said they were being used in the ground and then it stopped. Can you tell us what you were about to say, please.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes. The weapons were being use against ground targets rather than airborne targets for which they were designed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did these weapons have a specific mode that would allow them to be used in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, although the weapons were designed to work in high-elevation angles, it was possible, or is possible, to depress the barrels of these weapons so that they can, in fact, be used to engage ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the occasion when you saw these guns, were they, in fact, in this suppressed mode?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, they were. You have to understand that generally, around Sarajevo, there were no aircraft movements. These weapons represented a highly effective tool to be used in the offensive role and so understandably they were being used against ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would be a military use of a triple-A gun in the ground mode?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: If I understand the question, do you mean how would I use it in the ground mode?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It is very unlikely that as a British troop, I would ever use anti-aircraft weapons in the ground mode unless the situation was dire or an emergency because the ammunition is specifically designed really for engaging aircraft. And the ammunition is extremely expensive. If any air threats exist, then any normal commander would be loath to use those guns and the ammunition in the ground role, but would indeed reserve it for potential air threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What made the type of rounds fired by a triple-A gun unique or why were they so expensive?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: They are not necessarily unique. They are expensive, in terms of unit financial cost and also in terms of logistic impact, because they are large and they are heavy and they are difficult to move around. But the rounds themselves are extremely high velocity and they generally have an explosive warhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is the approximate calibre of these rounds?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft weapons vary enormously in calibre, from 12.7 millimetres up to 100 millimetres plus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate barrel size of the weapons that you saw on the VRS lines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My experience told me that they were probably 30 millimetre plus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of effect would result from firing a triple-A gun in the ground mode?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: From the point of view of the gunner, of the user, a very satisfying effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Because the rounds are accurate within limits. Because they are high velocity and because they have an explosive warhead, the effect on target would be large. Far greater than a normal calibre, or a similar calibre weapon, firing solid ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, if in the next few minutes you could find a suitable to have the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was about to move on to shelling so perhaps this would be a most convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then have a break until 6.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 6 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, I would like to turn your attention now to incidents involving artillery and, specifically, shelling of the city of Sarajevo. Did there come a time when you personally witnessed any artillery shells impacting the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Throughout my stay in Sarajevo, on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall a specific occasion when you witnessed a shelling incident from the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I witnessed a number of shelling incidents from the PTT building. It was possible to stand on the roof of the building or on the fire escape and within a few minutes, it would be easy to witness shells impacting somewhere in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me take your attention to an incident you described in your statement, involving a civilian dwelling being struck by artillery. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, amongst others. I think it stands out because of the unexpectedness, and because of the relative devastation that one round appeared to cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I believe it would have been late November or December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you witnessed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: As I recall, I was inside the PTT building. Considering where I was, I think I was probably, either finishing or just about to commence my lunch and I was looking out of the window, across to the north to the feature known as Zuc. As I looked out of the window, all seemed quiet. There was very little happening at that time. And before my eyes, one of the dwellings, the civilian houses, on the side of the hill simply disintegrated into a ball of flame and smoke, in front of my eyes. This is some 600 to 800 metres, possibly a bit more, from where I was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the flames or smoke dissipated, what did you see on the spot where the house had been located?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There was nothing there, other than the remnants of the building. There was no indication to me, or indeed during the subsequent follow-up by a Papa team, that there had been any specific target of a military value there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific findings of the Papa team with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: As I recall, as a result of that incident two people were killed, two civilians. That is the report that came back as a result of the Papa team's on-the-ground investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any incident reports with respect to the outgoing fire or the source of fire that impacted that house?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I do. On this occasion, I made my way back to the operations room, from where I had moved to have my lunch. A colleague was covering the operations desk at the time, and there had been a report from the Lukavica team, Lima team, of a report of outgoing fire which coincided, almost to the second, with the impact which was observed on Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time you saw the house being destroyed on Zuc, which military force controlled the area encompassing Zuc Hill?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The -- well the area encompassing Zuc Hill was split more or less centrally. There was a very distinct line of trenches running across the hill, and so it was separated between Bosnian and Serb forces. But the point of impact of this particular round was very well within the Bosnian-held area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how close the house was that you saw being destroyed to these trenches?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was more than 1.000 metres, a lot more. The nearest front line to that house ran some 1.500 metres to the west, and then came back across onto the line of Zuc Hill but was effectively in dead ground, i.e., behind the brow of the hill from that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were stationed in Sarajevo, did you become aware of any incoming mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I became very aware of it. It was occurring on an hourly basis, what we believed to be mortar fire, although it wasn't always possible to differentiate between artillery and mortar fire at the point of impact. There were countless examples of mortar fire which I personally witnessed, both the mortar fire itself, the impacts and the aftermath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you able to draw any general conclusions about the use of mortars against the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Not specifically, other than the fact that mortars were being used because we had witnessed from our Lima teams mortars being fired and we were able to assess that some of the ordinance that was impacting inside Sarajevo was indeed mortar ammunition, rather than artillery ammunition and quite a lot of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did it seem to you, based on your experience in Sarajevo, that this mortar fire was being used in a coordinated military -- effective Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military attack?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I saw examples of indirect fire, both artillery and mortars, being used in an extremely well-coordinated, professional fashion against what were obviously specific targets. Normally, around the areas of the front line. There was no doubt in my mind that the operators of those weapons were proficient and had good drills and communications. One particular example which I could cite, which, again, I recall occurred in late October was where indirect fire was being use to support what appeared to be an infantry attack and there was also coordinated illumination these are special -- this is special ammunition which is fired from mortars and guns to illuminate an area of operations at night. The combined effect of the mortar and artillery fire and illumination being coordinated, led me to think that the people, or what I was witnessing was extremely professionally executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also see examples where mortar fire was being used against other than specific targets, as you have put it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes. The -- within Sarajevo throughout that period there was what I would term "general background activity" throughout any one 24-hour period. For example, one would experience general impacting of indirect fire within the city. And this was very different from the coordinated, sustained attacks on specific targets that I have mentioned. These rounds on this -- these incidents appeared to be essentially random, often single rounds fired from artillery or mortar weapons without any kind of follow-up action, which, in respect to indirect fire weapons, is very unusual. Generally, with an indirect fire weapon, it is very difficult to hit a specific target, if not impossible to hit a specific target, with one round. These weapons by their nature are what we term, "area weapons" and they are designed to cover an area of ground with fire. They are not of any real use used individually, one at a time, firing one round. Even if a weapon has been accurately sited and accurately adjusted on to a target, atmospheric conditions will change throughout any given period, be it temperature, wind speed, or humidity and this will affect greatly the accuracy of that weapon so that you could never guarantee where a round is going to land. Therefore, to fire one round and not follow it up or adjust it on to a target would seem pointless, in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does this type of tactic that you just described, does this have any type of generally accepted military term for this type of attack?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The only situation on which I could imagine advocate the use of such weapons in such a manner, would be to generally suppress or harass a large area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, during the time period that you were in Sarajevo, did you ever see or hear any type of multiple launched rocket system attacks on the city?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My experience and reports that came in from my colleagues suggested very strongly that, indeed, rockets of some type were indeed used in or against Sarajevo during my period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any specific knowledge of instances in which you saw or heard such rockets impacting Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Again, if we go back to October 1993, in that time frame, there had been reports coming in from our military observers on the Lima side of rocket-launched systems having been sighted. We indeed had reports or IncReps coming in that indicated from our Papa observation post that rockets had been fired. On one occasion I am fairly confident that I witnessed a rocket attack be it not visually, but certainly orally, because the characteristics of a rocket attack are somewhat different to the characteristics of say, normal indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say orally, are you stating that you heard this?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is right. The -- as I say, I heard characteristics of fire that would -- that led me to believe that I was actually witnessing a rocket attack, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you have been in the British armed forces, have you trained on these type of rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I have not trained on them personally, but I have witnessed them firing and I have been on the ground where they have impacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is the military use of these type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There are a number of uses, depending upon the calibre and the range of such systems. But in general terms and as far as I am aware, with regard to the types of systems that were probably used in Bosnia at that time, the main purpose is to cause a rapid and devastating effect on the target. On an area target, these weapons are not accurate by any stretch of the imagination. They are designed to cause a great psychological effect upon the troops or the targets against which they are used. But they are not generally used in close support as they cannot be trusted to hit specific targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Hermer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, since you are standing, do I take it you will be cross-examine the witness? You will be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Hermer.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will allow myself to ask my questions in French. You now have the rank of major, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you are a military person, that is your career, you are a career soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Major, to become a career soldier, as you are, could you briefly give us some information on what is necessary in relation to your training, that is on your didactic [Realtime transcript read in error "dactic"] from training?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I didn't understand the word "dactic", sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Didactic. Pedagogical training.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes. In my own personal case, I first joined the ranks as a soldier. Underwent basic military and specialist commando training from the age of 16. At the rank of corporal, at the age of 21, I was commissioned as an officer. I returned to a training environment and was subjected to a further 24 months of intensive military and commando training. Upon the completion of which, I was posted to a Royal Marine commando unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Do you wish me to go into specific detail regarding the training I received?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. In order to become a major and a career soldier officer, did you never receive or discord in certain military schools, did you have any historic training, a historic background training, theoretical training?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, a large amount of my training was theoretical, studying past conflicts, political and military interaction. I also attended staff college in 1997 where this theory was taken to a much higher level. In particular, we studied operations at brigade and divisional level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer, Witness. I would also like to ask you, therefore, some questions regarding your competencies in theory and in history, but for the moment, let us go back to Sarajevo and to Mount Igman. Could you please tell us during your stay in Sarajevo what was the army which controlled the heights of Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: When I arrived in late or mid-August 1993 the heights of Mount Igman which, if I'm right, are known as Bijelasnice, were not controlled by any army other than UNPROFOR. The army of the Serb Krajina-- my apologies -- of the Republika Srpska was essentially to the east and the north and west of Mount Igman whilst the United Nations were controlling the gap between the Serbian forces and the Bosnian forces which encompassed the heights of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. How many observation posts were there in that area of Mount Igman during the time while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I assume you are referring to military observer, UNMO, observation posts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what time, Witness, if that is the case, was Mount Igman, and I mean the heights, mounts of Mount Igman were under the control of the Muslim army, that is, the so-called Sarajevo army?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The answer to that is, that during my tenure, the heights of Mount Igman were not controlled by the so-called Sarajevo army. There was a company of UN troops, either French Foreign Legion or French Marines who occupied that area throughout my stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that, at a certain moment, some troops of the Muslim army were able to gain advantage, military strategic advantage to position themselves on the slopes, if we can use that term, on Mount Igman, and if that was so, when was that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Throughout my time on Igman and throughout the time of my colleagues who were there subsequent to me on Mount Igman there were incursions of the so-called UN controlled area and by both sides. You are right in saying that, at one stage, Bosnian army troops did occupy areas of Mount Igman that, according to the agreement, they should not have, but it is always fair to say, I think that there were incursions, in the form of fighting patrols by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for this answer, Witness. Isn't it true that there was a battle that was fought in order to gain or to keep, to maintain the control of Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There was. There were battles fought over Mount Igman because, obviously, it was strategically a very important territory. Throughout my tenure, however, the United Nations retained a presence on that mountain and although perhaps not 100 per cent effective in controlling it and denying it, I would not go so far as to say that either side effectively controlled that narrow corridor across Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But since you are telling us that the UN personnel had an effective presence there, could you tell us which brigade of the Muslim army were positioned at the time on Mount Igman or around it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My memory in these matters and specifics is not 100 per cent clear. I recall a so-called Bosnian Mountain Brigade. I say "so-called" because in normal military terms, this was not a brigade, who had a headquarters up on the area of Mount Igman, but out with the area controlled by the United Nations. As for other units up there. The specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will just stop you here, in order not to waste time. So you said that there were HQ and you are talking about the HQ of the Muslim army, if it is possible, can you just answer with a yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I can't answer that with a yes or no, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you know or did you not know as a military observer and as a major, which was the -- which was which side had HQ there? Were they Serbs or were there Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: They were Muslims, but the phrase you used --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You can continue your description, please, major.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Thank you. The term you used was "Bosnian army headquarters." It was not an army headquarters. There was an headquarters element located on the mountain, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel. Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am taking note of that, Witness, but if you could continue with what you were going to say before I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No, I am sorry I have to look back through the text. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were talking about headquarters and you said as far as other units up there, the specific -- that is where you ended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as other units operating in that area, the specific titles of those units I can't remember in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You were talking about units and I am talking about brigades. There is a difference. You do not remember any more about Muslim brigades which were at the time on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Not from memory, not without --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Would you please confirm, Witness, if the following is the case: The number of 105-millimetre cannons which were in the region under the control of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you confirm, Witness, the number of 102-millimetre cannons that were under the control of that army in 122-millimetre cannons that were in control of that army and that region?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you confirm, Witness, of the -- of the rocket launchers that were held by that army at that time in that region?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us the same answer or no answer regarding the Howitzer, the 130-millimetre cannon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Hermer, do you have any specific knowledge on numbers of heavy weaponry in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specific knowledge, no. Other than what we saw, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No specific numbers. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I asked another line of questioning. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, on several occasions involved in missions on that region in that area that we are talking about, that is on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I would like to you please define "mission."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can be very precise in fact. I believe that you were on mission of the United Nations, but perhaps I could rephrase the question. Were you at any time, in any capacity, on Mount Igman during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was on Mount Igman for approximately 20 days in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: 20 days out of how many days, please, in total?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: My entire stay in Sarajevo was just a little more than five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So would you agree with me if I said that that was approximately 150 days then?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That would be a fair approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... approximately 150 days, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: During those 20 days that are approximately about 20 per cent of your time, you have never seen a weapon of those that I mentioned earlier, on those heights above Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: If you are talking about Bosnian weapons, yes, many.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am talking about the weapons which I mentioned earlier, precise weapons I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Some of those calibres, weapons were present, that is, true, they were present on the mountain --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which ones. Which ones, could you please tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: They had the Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: A total number I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: More than four, more than five, for instance, more than six?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Less than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And perhaps more than three. So for the other weapons, please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The 120-millimetre mortar that you mentioned, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: These weapons were more abundant. These weapons were -- I viewed these weapons regularly. There were a number of them, a specific number again --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will have to interrupt you. When you say "specific number so what do you think approximately how many were there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Again, because these weapons are mobile, it is impossible for me to say, but -- I can't give you a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: More than, less than?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, these weapons were used in a fixed way, the 120-millimetres?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: These weapons, the ones that I saw, were often in a fixed position, what we would call a "gun line." But I have no doubt that they were moved regularly so they were not permanently fixed, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. You saw these weapons on several occasions and several locations, so when -- the crews that were serving these mortars, were they different?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was not possible to view the crews. Often these weapons were unattended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am going to go back to other weapons, 105 and 122. What would you say about them?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The 105-millimetre I don't recall. Are you talking of the 122 Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. I was talking about what is called in Serbian cannons, 122-millimetre cannons. I don't think they are Howitzers. These are field guns, probably.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I again don't recall having seen field guns of that calibre on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you have seen field guns of a different calibre, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Not up on Mount Igman, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You spoke, Witness, earlier about a gun line and these weapons would have been placed on a gun line and this gun line would be positioned between what and what else?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: The nature of the gun line, gun lines that I witnessed, were on hard flat ground without any overhead obstructions obviously placed in a location whereby they could be brought to bear rapidly onto a target. They weren't placed between anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness could you please tell us if this is the case and since you went there: What was, strategically speaking, the view that the observers were able to have, either from Mount Igman on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I am sorry, do you mean the physical view?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When I say "view" I don't just mean the physical view, of course, but also strategic view. That dominating point from a military point of view, if there was any?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: There was a strategic view which was gained by the military observers on that mountain. The physical view as you have referred to it, was limited, but the overall view which that observation team gave us was, we believed, important at the time because Mount Igman was the strategic entry point --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will have to interrupt you here, please. I wanted you to tell us, if that was the case, whether you could just confirm by a yes or no whether from Mount Igman it was possible to have a dominating strategic position viewing therefore the entire city from above?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Certainly from the area which I have frequented --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I don't think you understood my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please clarify yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hadn't finished, certainly from the area where I was located and frequented, there was no view whatsoever. However, I paid one visit to the top of the highest point. From there the view was significantly better, but did not give a good view of the whole of Sarajevo, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the armies. Could you tell us how many soldiers -- how many soldiers were deployed by the Muslim army in by the Sarajevo Sector?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I am assuming that -- that you are referring to Mount Igman and therefore I will say that it was difficult to be specific. People, commanders, were not forthcoming when asked to divulge numbers of men and it was not possible to carry out a detailed head count of the troops involved. But I would say not a significant number in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The last thing on this point: You spoke about heavy artillery. The troops that you saw, did they also have light artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: We are talking now about Bosnian troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, still.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: On Mount Igman, I can't recall having seen specific light artillery, I presume, you are talk about calibres of 105 millimetres or below, although there were a significant number of mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I was asking the question whether Muslim army soldiers had a light weapons, the Kalashnikov and so on?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry. I thought you said artillery. The answer to that is: Yes, they had small arms weapons, machine-guns and even, what I would term "civilian weapons", shotguns and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What do you mean by the weapons? I am just going to check in the transcript. What do you mean by "civilian weapons"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: By that term I refer to weapons that are not of -- generally regarded to be of a military specification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For instance?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: A hunting gun, firing shot rather than bullets, or a civilian hunting rifle, that sort of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So many soldiers were armed with such weapons of a civilian character?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Not many, no, but they were notable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Among the soldiers that we are talking about now what was their situation in relation to how they were dressed? Uniforms, did they have uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: No, not what I would regard to be complete military uniforms. A number of them were wearing possibly one item of military clothing, a jacket or trousers and no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: However, these people had weapons, they were able to carry weapons, to be armed?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major, for this answer. Since we have asked these questions in relation to Mount Igman, I would now like to ask you a more general question and whether would your answer also apply to other areas in the theater, so to speak, as far as you were able to find out and to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, all the questions you asked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I am talking about the very last question, the weapons in relation to the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you are talking about the civilian weapons and the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that certainly applied in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, we had here testimonies regarding the fact that very young people would visit certain military facilities and installations, apparently in the hope that they would find food there. Did you see yourself, did you know about such facts?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly witnessed on a number of occasions, as you term it, "very young people," around military installations. Whether they were looking for food or not, I don't know, but there were often young children around military positions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you say, Witness, "young people" am I to conclude from your answer that we are talking about people below the military age?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Considering, I think, it was difficult to define the military age in that theater, these people were very young and certainly below the age of 16, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Major, as you are a professional soldier, did it happen occasionally, did you see people that is, children below 16 years of age, who were even, lato sensu, bringing assistance to the military personnel there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: If you include in the term "assistance" carrying out errands and small tasks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was this very frequent or relatively frequent?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: It was common place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Major. You said "small errands." Could you perhaps clarify this and tell us briefly what you mean by "small errands" by just giving us two or three examples. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I don't know if I can give you three examples, but the sort of thing which I witnessed was small children bringing food supplies to the soldiers, possibly cleaning their equipment for them, in return, I assume for a small reward, who knows. And generally doing the types of labour-intensive, mundane tasks you wouldn't normally give to a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for what you said, Witness. So cleaning the equipment, that would also mean oiling weapons or checking the cleanliness of canons and et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: I do not specifically recall children cleaning or maintaining weaponry. I did see children with weapons, but not necessarily cleaning them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which weapons, Witness? Or what type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Small arms, personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Guns?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY PETER HERMER
utterances.text: Rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know how long we are -- we can go on and considering that what we have to do, I believe that this would be an excellent moment to stop, but I can continue, if you wish

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... so therefore, if this is a suitable moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we will adjourn. But before adjourning, may I ask you one question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in your observation made at approximately half past 5.00, did you give a small yellow paper to those who are assisting us?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked -- you made a small comment on the transcript and especially the French, that is what at 17:31.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If I gave a small yellow paper to someone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a small yellow paper as I indicated before that we could give to the people doing the transcript so that we can guide them and at least assist them in performing their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a number of information that I have to do, however, it is mostly white but I suppose I will do it immediately, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow, but not the usual time, due to some initial appearances. We will start at a quarter to 3.00. So we will adjourn in this same courtroom and I cannot guarantee that we will be able to start at a quarter to 3.00 because it depends on the time the initial appearances would take. So, therefore, I have to ask for your patience, if we could not immediately start. Mr. Mundis? No. Then we will adjourn until tomorrow, same courtroom, at a quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th, day of May, 2002, at 2.45 p.m. 25
